steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Grasping is a basic skill for a lot of robotic applications, and many tasks cannot be done at all if the robot cannot manipulate objects well. In many cases the objects are not isolated, and then grasping gets hard because of occlusions and clutter in the environment. Humans are dexterous in these situations, and in the same way robots should use motion primitives such as pushing to separate the target object from the clutter so that it can be grasped. To grasp well, a robot has to integrate visual observations of the goal object(s) and understand the spatial relationships, not just execute a basic antipodal grasp. So all the components of the system have to work together. The sensory information the robot gets from the environment can be flawed, so it has to deal with these inconsistencies. Also the scene changes after each action, so the robot needs to adapt before the task is completed. On top of that, planning the motion of the manipulator to reach the desired pose is hard in itself and needs continuous observation of the environment and adjustments.

- Our focus
  - self-supervised learning of pushing and grasping in clutter through DRL (cite)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Grasping is a basic skill for a lot of robotic applications, and many tasks cannot be done at all if the robot cannot manipulate objects well. In many cases the objects are not isolated, and then grasping gets hard because of occlusions and clutter in the environment. Humans are dexterous in these situations, and in the same way robots should use motion primitives such as pushing to separate the target object from the clutter so that it can be grasped. To grasp well, a robot has to integrate visual observations of the goal object(s) and understand the spatial relationships, not just execute a basic antipodal grasp. So all the components of the system have to work together. The sensory information the robot gets from the environment can be flawed, so it has to deal with these inconsistencies. Also the scene changes after each action, so the robot needs to adapt before the task is completed. On top of that, planning the motion of the manipulator to reach the desired pose is hard in itself and needs continuous observation of the environment and adjustments.

In this paper we mainly look at self-supervised learning for pushing and grasping in cluttered settings using DRL. As shown in Fig. 1, when the target object cannot be grasped directly, our method uses a combination of pushing and grasping to make sure the manipulation succeeds. Many studies have looked at combining pushing and grasping and how the two together affect object manipulation. Most of these studies focus on bin-picking tasks, where objects are moved from one bin to another, but our work looks at situations where the clutter around the target object makes it ungraspable at first. When pushing and grasping interact, they give a unified behavior and object manipulation gets better. If pushing and grasping are treated as separate actions, this can lead to unforeseen changes in the scene and makes the problem harder to solve, so instead our method uses DRL to use the synergy between them and deal with its limitations. The whole system architecture is shown in Fig. 2 and described in Section III. Our contributions are the following:

- We propose a self-supervised learning method that lets a service robot learn pushing and grasping policies at the same time, with the goal of clearing occlusions around target objects efficiently. The approach handles complex tasks like obstacle removal, and we also look at the constraints of the model and the system.

- We run extensive simulations and real-world experiments to validate the method. The simulations include scenarios with building blocks in packed and in random arrangements. Experiments with the real robot also confirm that the approach is robust. The results outperform current state-of-the-art strategies in task completion and grasp success rates, as detailed in Section IV.

- We make our source code and trained models publicly available so that others can replicate the results.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Grasping is fundamental to many robotic applications, and it makes possible tasks that are untenable without adept object manipulation [1]. In many situations, objects are not isolated, which makes grasping challenging due to environmental occlusions and clutter [2,3,4]. Taking inspiration from human dexterity, robots should use motion primitives, like pushing, to isolate target objects from clutter and facilitate grasping [5,6]. For effective grasping, robots need to integrate visual observations of the goal object(s) and understand spatial relationships, rather than only executing a basic antipodal grasp. This requires a harmonious system in which all components work together [7]. Given the potentially flawed sensory information a robot obtains from its environment, it needs to address these inconsistencies effectively. In addition, the scene changes dynamically after each action, which requires the robot to adapt before the task is completed [8]. Moreover, planning the manipulator's motion to reach the desired pose is inherently challenging and requires continuous observation of the environment and adjustments [9,10,11,12,13,4].

This paper mainly addresses self-supervised learning for pushing and grasping in cluttered settings through DRL [14,15,16]. As depicted in Fig. 1, when a direct grasp of the target object is not feasible, our method combines pushing and grasping to guarantee successful manipulation. Many studies have explored the combination of pushing and grasping and their joint impact on object manipulation [17,18,19]. While most existing studies focus on bin-picking tasks, which involve transferring objects between bins, our work investigates situations where the surrounding clutter makes the target object initially ungraspable. The interplay between pushing and grasping produces a unified behavior that improves the proficiency of object manipulation [20,21]. Instead of treating pushing and grasping as separate actions, which can lead to unforeseen scene changes and problem-solving hurdles, our method uses DRL to harness their synergy and address its limitations. The complete system architecture is shown in Fig. 2 and detailed in Section III. Broadly, our paper makes the following contributions:

- We propose a self-supervised learning method that enables a service robot to learn pushing and grasping policies concurrently, aiming to efficiently clear occlusions around target objects. Our approach addresses complex tasks like obstacle removal while probing the constraints of the model and system.

- We conduct extensive simulations and real-world experiments to validate our method. Simulations include scenarios with building blocks in both packed and random arrangements. Empirical studies with the real robot further confirm the robustness of our approach. The results clearly outperform current state-of-the-art strategies in task completion and grasp success rates, as detailed in Section IV.

- For the benefit of the research community, we make our source code and trained models publicly available to facilitate replication of the results.
